prompt: `aws_subnet.app` has `count = 3`. What is the address of the first subnet?
hint: The index starts where most programming languages start it.

choices.text: `aws_subnet.app[1]`
choices.why: That is the second copy: `count.index` starts at zero.

choices.text: `aws_subnet.app.first`
choices.why: There is no such attribute; a copy is reached by its index in square brackets.

choices.text: `aws_subnet.app[0]`
choices.why: Yes. The copies are numbered from zero, and the apply printed `aws_subnet.app[0]: Creating...`.

choices.text: `aws_subnet.app-0`
choices.why: A hyphen would be part of a name; the index goes in square brackets after the resource's address.

prompt: Why is `count` called a meta-argument rather than an argument of `aws_subnet`?
hint: Who reads it: Terraform or the AWS provider?

choices.text: Because the AWS API takes a number of copies in one call
choices.why: The provider never sees `count`; it receives one subnet per copy.

choices.text: Terraform reads it itself, before the provider sees anything
choices.why: Right. It is handled before the provider sees anything, so it means the same on every resource type.

choices.text: Because it is written first in the block, by convention
choices.why: Putting it first is a readability habit; the name comes from who interprets it.

choices.text: Because the state stores it beside each subnet
choices.why: What the state keeps is one entry per address; `count` itself is not what makes it a meta-argument.

prompt: `count = var.public ? 1 : 0` on a gateway, and an output reads `aws_internet_gateway.shop[0].id`. What happens when `public` is false?
hint: Look at what `aws_internet_gateway.shop` holds when there are no copies.

choices.text: The output becomes an empty string
choices.why: Terraform does not invent a value for a missing element; the lesson's plan stopped with an error.

choices.text: Terraform keeps the old gateway
choices.why: A reference does not keep a resource alive; the plan did list the gateway for destruction before failing.

choices.text: The plan stops with `Invalid index`
choices.why: Yes. The list is empty, so `[0]` points at nothing; `one(aws_internet_gateway.shop[*].id)` copes with zero.

choices.text: Terraform creates the gateway anyway
choices.why: `count` decides how many copies exist; a reference cannot raise it.

prompt: Inside a block with `count`, the number of the copy being built, starting at zero, is `count.___`.
hint: The name a list position has in most languages.

prompt: Three subnets were made with `count` from a list of three ranges. The middle range is removed. What does the plan do to `aws_subnet.app[1]`?
hint: Which range does index 1 point at after the removal?

choices.text: Replaces it, because its argument is now the third range
choices.why: Its argument became the third range, and a subnet's range forces replacement.

choices.text: Destroys it, since it held the removed range
choices.why: Terraform matches by address, not by range; the destroyed one was `[2]`, out of range for count.

choices.text: Leaves it alone, since only the list changed
choices.why: The list feeds the block: `var.subnets[1]` is now a different range.

choices.text: Updates its range in place
choices.why: A subnet's range cannot be edited in place; the plan marked it `# forces replacement`.

prompt: In the lesson's plan for removing the middle subnet, how many resources were to be destroyed?
hint: The summary line counts a replacement as both an add and a destroy.

prompt: Which edit to a list used with `count` leaves every existing subnet untouched?
hint: Which change moves no existing index?

choices.text: Sorting the list so the ranges read in order
choices.why: Sorting can move every element, and each moved copy is replaced.

choices.text: Inserting a new range at the front of the list
choices.why: Every existing element moves up one index.

choices.text: Adding a range at the end
choices.why: Yes. No existing index moves, so the plan only adds a copy.

choices.text: Removing the first range from the list
choices.why: Every element after it moves down a place.

prompt: A list of three bucket names drives `count`, and the name only goes into a tag, which can be changed in place. The middle name is removed. What does the plan show?
hint: Nothing forces replacement here.

choices.text: Nothing, because a tag is not part of the resource's identity
choices.why: The tag of copy `[1]` changes value, so the plan has to show it.

choices.text: An update to `[1]` and a destroy of `[2]`
choices.why: Right. Copy `[1]` quietly takes the third name and the third copy goes, which is harder to notice than a replacement.

choices.text: One destroy of the copy whose tag held the removed name
choices.why: That is what `for_each` would do; `count` matches by position.

choices.text: A replacement of both `[1]` and `[2]`
choices.why: A tag change is an in-place update, and `[2]` has no element left, so it is destroyed rather than replaced.

prompt: With `for_each = { web = "10.20.1.0/24", db = "10.20.3.0/24" }`, what is `each.value` in the copy for `db`?
hint: Key on the left, value on the right.

choices.why: That is `each.key`.

choices.text: `1`, its position in the map
choices.why: A map has no positions that `for_each` uses; that is the point of it.
Yes: the value on the right of the key.

choices.text: The whole map, so each copy can see the others
choices.why: Each copy sees one entry: `each.key` and `each.value`.

prompt: Why does `for_each = ["10.30.0.0/16", "10.31.0.0/16"]` fail, while the same values wrapped in `toset(...)` work?
hint: What would name each copy?

choices.text: A list's elements have no name but their position
choices.why: Right. A set of strings uses the strings themselves as keys; a list would bring position back.

choices.text: Lists of more than one network range are rejected by the AWS provider
choices.why: The provider never saw it: the error came from Terraform reading `for_each`.

choices.text: `toset` converts the ranges to numbers Terraform can count
choices.why: The elements stay strings; they become the keys.

choices.text: Square brackets are reserved for `count` in HCL
choices.why: Square brackets write any list or tuple; the error said it was given a tuple.

prompt: In a resource with `for_each` over a map, the name on the left of the current entry is `each.___`.
hint: The other one is `each.value`.

prompt: Ana rewrites three `count` subnets as `for_each` and changes nothing else. Without `moved` blocks, what does the plan propose?
hint: Terraform matches on addresses.

choices.text: Nothing, since the ranges are identical
choices.why: Terraform does not compare ranges to work out identity; the old addresses simply vanished from the file.

choices.text: Three in-place renames
choices.why: An address is not a property of the subnet in AWS; there is nothing to update there.

choices.text: Three destroys and three creates
choices.why: Yes: `Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy.`, each destroy because the resource does not use count.

choices.text: An error asking for `state mv`
choices.why: Terraform plans the change happily; that is why it has to be read.

prompt: What does applying a plan made only of `has moved to` lines change in AWS?
hint: Where do addresses live?

choices.text: It retags each subnet with its new key
choices.why: The plan showed no tag changes; the summary was 0 to change.

choices.text: Nothing: only the state's addresses change
choices.why: Right. It rewrites the addresses in the state; the subnets keep their ids.

choices.text: It recreates the subnets one at a time
choices.why: No subnet is recreated: the ids in the plan are the ones from the original apply.

choices.text: It moves them into the VPC named in the block
choices.why: A `moved` block names two addresses and nothing else; no VPC is involved.

prompt: Put the steps for changing a live `count` resource to `for_each` without replacing anything in order.
hint: Read the plan before you trust it.
items: Rewrite the block with `for_each` over a map
Write one `moved` block per old index
Run `terraform plan` and check every line says `has moved to`
Apply, and confirm `terraform state list` shows the keys
trap: Applying before reading the plan is the slip: a wrong pairing shows up there as a replacement.

prompt: Ana pairs `aws_subnet.app[0]` (10.20.1.0/24) with `aws_subnet.app["app"]`, whose range in the file is 10.20.2.0/24. What does the plan show for that subnet?
hint: The move happens first; then the file is compared with what was moved.

choices.text: A move, and then a replacement because the range differs
choices.why: Right. Terraform moves it and then finds the range wrong, which forces replacement. A correct move plans nothing.

choices.text: A move with no changes
choices.why: The file asks for 10.20.2.0/24 at that address and the subnet has 10.20.1.0/24.

choices.text: An error, since Terraform checks that a moved block keeps the same range
choices.why: Terraform checks the addresses, not what the resource holds.

choices.text: An in-place update of the range
choices.why: A subnet's range cannot be updated in place.

prompt: Inside `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.web_ports ... }`, how does `content` refer to the current port?
hint: The variable is named after the block.

choices.text: `each.value`
choices.why: `each` belongs to a resource-level `for_each`; a dynamic block names its iterator after itself.

choices.text: `ingress.value`
choices.why: Yes; `iterator` can rename it.

choices.text: `var.web_ports.value`
choices.why: That is the whole list, which has no `value` attribute.

choices.text: `count.index`
choices.why: No `count` is involved, and an index would give the position rather than the port.

prompt: Port 8443 is added to a list feeding a `dynamic "ingress"` block. Why does the plan list five rules, two going out and three coming in?
hint: Where do the rules live?

choices.text: The dynamic block replaces the whole security group on every change
choices.why: The plan said `update in-place` and `0 to add`; the group is kept.

choices.text: They are one set inside one resource, compared whole
choices.why: Right. The reviewer has to spot by eye that only 8443 is new; separate rule resources make it one line.

choices.text: The ports were sorted, which shifted every index
choices.why: The list was appended to, not sorted; the display comes from comparing a set.

choices.text: moto rejected the first two rules and they must be created again
choices.why: This was a plan; nothing had been sent to moto yet.

prompt: Which statements about `dynamic` blocks match the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are true.

choices.text: They generate nested blocks, which cannot take `count` or `for_each` themselves
choices.why: That is what they are for.

choices.text: Their `for_each` accepts a list
choices.why: Unlike the resource-level argument; `ingress.key` is then the index.

choices.text: Each generated block gets its own address in the state
choices.why: The blocks live inside one resource with one address; separate rule resources are what get addresses.

choices.text: Mixing inline `ingress` with `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` on one group makes them undo each other
choices.why: Each style tries to own the full set of rules.

choices.text: They are the preferred way to write security group rules in the AWS provider
choices.why: The provider's documentation recommends the separate rule resources.

prompt: A configuration has `provider "aws" { region = "sa-east-1" }` and `provider "aws" { alias = "us", region = "us-east-2" }`. A bucket has no `provider` argument. Where is it created?
hint: Which block is the default?

choices.text: In `us-east-2`, the last provider block declared in the files
choices.why: Order of declaration does not matter; the block without an alias is the default.

choices.text: In `sa-east-1`
choices.why: Yes. Only resources that say `provider = aws.us` use the alias.

choices.text: In both regions, one copy each
choices.why: A provider block is a connection, not a copy machine; that would take two resources.

choices.text: Nowhere: Terraform asks which one to use
choices.why: There is no ambiguity to ask about; the unaliased block is the default.

prompt: With version 6 of the AWS provider, when is a provider alias still needed instead of the resource's `region` argument?
hint: What else does a provider block carry besides a region?

choices.text: When the bucket name has to be unique across regions
choices.why: Bucket names are a matter for S3, not for how Terraform connects.

choices.text: When the resource goes to `us-east-2`
choices.why: The lesson's `logs` bucket used `region = "us-east-2"` and landed there.

choices.text: When the second configuration is another account, role or set of credentials
choices.why: Right. Credentials, roles and `default_tags` are provider settings a resource argument cannot change.

choices.text: When there are more than two regions in one configuration
choices.why: The number of regions does not matter; what differs between them does.

prompt: A teammate deletes the `provider "aws" { alias = "us" ... }` block while the backup bucket it created still exists. What happens on the next plan?
hint: A resource remembers which configuration created it.

choices.text: The bucket moves to `sa-east-1` with the default provider
choices.why: Terraform cannot move a bucket between regions, and it does not switch a resource's provider silently.

choices.text: Terraform plans to destroy the bucket as an orphan
choices.why: To destroy it Terraform would need the configuration that reaches it, which is gone.

choices.text: An error saying that configuration is still required
choices.why: Yes: `Provider configuration not present`. Re-add the alias, remove the resources, then the alias.

choices.text: Nothing, because the resource block still names `aws.us`
choices.why: Naming an alias nobody declares is exactly what fails.

prompt: Match each situation to the tool the lesson's table gives it.
hint: One option is left over.

pairs.left: A resource that exists only when a flag is true
Subnets that each have a role
Nested blocks with no resource of their own

prompt: `for_each = toset(values(aws_subnet.app)[*].id)` fails on the first plan. Why?
hint: When does AWS invent a subnet id?

choices.text: Subnet ids contain hyphens, which are not allowed in keys
choices.why: Any string can be a key; the trouble is that these strings do not exist yet.

choices.text: AWS invents subnet ids at apply, so the keys are unknown while planning
choices.why: Right. Iterate over `aws_subnet.app`, whose keys Ana wrote, and use `each.value.id`.

choices.text: `toset` cannot convert a list of ids
choices.why: `toset` converts lists of strings; the error was about unknown values.

choices.text: A route table association cannot use `for_each` at all
choices.why: The fixed version used `for_each = aws_subnet.app` on the same resource type.

prompt: Which of these does lesson 6, not this lesson, teach?
hint: The family of meta-arguments has five members.

choices.text: `provider`, to send a resource to another region
choices.why: That was this lesson's `provider-aliases` section.

choices.text: `for_each`, to name copies by key
choices.why: That was this lesson.

choices.text: `lifecycle`
choices.why: Yes, with `depends_on`: what happens to a resource over time.

choices.text: `count`, as an on/off switch with `? 1 : 0`
choices.why: That was this lesson's first section.

prompt: Ten IAM users are created with `count` from a list sorted by name. A new hire, Bruno, is added and the list is sorted again. What does the plan do to the users after Bruno?
hint: A user's name is the identity AWS knows it by.

choices.text: Leaves them alone
choices.why: The names did not change, but their indexes did, and Terraform matches on the index.

choices.text: Gives each one a different name
choices.why: Right. Every copy after the insertion shifts by one, so each index now asks for a different name, and the last index is new.

choices.text: Adds Bruno at the end only
choices.why: He was sorted into the middle, not appended; only an append leaves the rest alone.

choices.text: Fails, since two copies cannot hold the same name during the plan
choices.why: The plan computes the shift without complaint; it is the reader who has to catch it.

prompt: A plan for a change described as "remove one subnet" ends with `1 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy`. Which conclusions are justified? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the summary with what was asked.

choices.text: A subnet that should stay is being replaced
choices.why: One add and one extra destroy is a replacement of something nobody asked to touch.

choices.text: The subnets look like `count` over a list
choices.why: That shape is the index problem's signature.

choices.text: Terraform has a bug in how it computes subnet ranges
choices.why: The plan does exactly what the addresses say.

choices.text: The plan is safe to apply because the totals still end at two subnets
choices.why: The count of subnets is right and the identity of one of them is not.

prompt: A module you publish switches a resource from `count` to `for_each` with `moved` blocks. Six months later a colleague wants to delete the `moved` blocks. What is the risk?
hint: Who else applies this configuration?

choices.text: None: once applied anywhere, the move is recorded for everybody
choices.why: Each state records its own moves; a user who has not upgraded still has the old addresses.

choices.text: Terraform refuses to plan a configuration without them
choices.why: It plans fine; the trouble is what it plans for states with old addresses.

choices.text: The subnets that were already moved get moved back
choices.why: Deleting a `moved` block moves nothing back; it only stops future moves.

choices.text: States that still hold `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]` get destroys and recreates on their next plan
choices.why: Right. Their states still hold `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`, and without the blocks the plan destroys and recreates.
